3. Exploring the CDM

David Sarrat González

Source: vignettes/book-03-explore.Rmd
book-03-explore.Rmd

What you will learn

Find the right fields, distinguish rows from people, and check numeric coverage.

You need: the client packages and the Opal login from Getting started. This chapter uses omop.gibleed.

Start this chapter 

library(dsOMOPClient)
conns <- ds.omop.login("https://localhost:8443", user = "administrator",
  password = "password", resource = "omop.gibleed", server = "site")$conns

Read metadata before selecting records

A table’s schema describes its fields, even when the table is empty. The metadata returned by ds.omop.columns() help you decide which field to use. We display only the rows and columns needed for each decision.

Metadata How to read it
cdm_datatype, is_date The field’s expected type and whether it represents a date.
is_blocked The field is unavailable for analytical extraction, for example free text or a source value.
is_quasi_identifier Values such as dates and ages could help identify someone; they remain private and releases are checked.
concept_role, fk_domain Whether a code is a standard target or source code, and which kind of concept it should reference.
is_extension The field is an addition to the standard CDM schema.
is_untyped_identifier The field looks like an identifier but has no recognised standard role.
is_sensitive The field is flagged as sensitive, for example free text or an original source value.
semantic_class The kind of field, such as concept or ordinary; this alone does not determine what can be released.

A FALSE flag is not permission to download rows. These flags describe fields; the server also checks the operation and the support for each result.

Separate what was observed from its value 

columns <- ds.omop.columns("observation", conns = conns)$site
subset(columns, column_name %in% c("observation_concept_id", "value_as_concept_id",
  "value_as_number", "value_as_string", "observation_date"),
  select = c(column_name, cdm_datatype, is_date, is_blocked))
column_name cdm_datatype is_date is_blocked
observation_concept_id integer FALSE FALSE
observation_date date TRUE FALSE
value_as_number float FALSE FALSE
value_as_string varchar(60) FALSE TRUE
value_as_concept_id Integer FALSE FALSE

observation_concept_id identifies what was observed; in a questionnaire it identifies the question. value_as_concept_id holds a coded value or answer, and value_as_number a numeric value. value_as_string is blocked free text. Selecting the observation and choosing its value field are separate decisions.

ds.omop.table.stats("observation", conns = conns)
#> <dsomop_result>
#> Servers: site
#> Scope: per_site
#>
#> $site
#> $rows
#> [1] 1475
#>
#> $persons
#> [1] 670

The bands begin at 1,475 rows and 670 people: one person can contribute several observations. These represent 1,475–1,479 rows and 670–674 people. GiBleed’s observations describe allergies and histories, not education answers. The questionnaire chapters use a separate dataset for those answers.

Find the visit date and setting 

columns <- ds.omop.columns("visit_occurrence", conns = conns)$site
subset(columns, column_name %in% c("visit_start_date", "visit_end_date",
  "visit_concept_id", "visit_type_concept_id"),
  select = c(column_name, cdm_datatype, is_date, is_blocked))
column_name cdm_datatype is_date is_blocked
visit_concept_id integer FALSE FALSE
visit_start_date date TRUE FALSE
visit_end_date date TRUE FALSE
visit_type_concept_id Integer FALSE FALSE

visit_start_date is when the visit started. visit_concept_id describes its setting, such as inpatient or outpatient. visit_type_concept_id describes where the record came from; use the setting field to select inpatient visits.

ds.omop.table.stats("visit_occurrence", conns = conns)
#> <dsomop_result>
#> Servers: site
#> Scope: per_site
#>
#> $site
#> $rows
#> [1] 1035
#>
#> $persons
#> [1] 890

The bands are 1,035–1,039 visits and 890–894 people. Repeated visits explain why rows exceed people; a visit count is not a study sample size.

Exercise 1: a coded cause does not guarantee a death record

Find the coded cause and death date. Then check whether the server can release a count of deaths.

Solution

columns <- ds.omop.columns("death", conns = conns)$site
subset(columns, column_name %in% c("death_date", "cause_concept_id", "cause_source_value"),
  select = c(column_name, cdm_datatype, is_date, is_blocked))
column_name cdm_datatype is_date is_blocked
death_date date TRUE FALSE
cause_concept_id integer FALSE FALSE
cause_source_value varchar(50) FALSE TRUE

cause_concept_id is the coded cause. cause_source_value is the original source code, for example an ICD code, and is blocked here. The date field’s existence does not establish that any deaths were recorded.

ds.omop.table.stats("death", conns = conns)
#> <dsomop_result>
#> Servers: site
#> Scope: per_site
#>
#> $site
#> list()

The empty response contains no count. The public GiBleed source has an empty death table; through DataSHIELD alone this response could also mean a small withheld count. Treat it as unavailable, rather than asserting zero deaths.

Exercise 2: distinguish dispensing from visits

Find the drug exposure dates and supply duration. Does supply duration establish that somebody took the medicine every day?

Solution

columns <- ds.omop.columns("drug_exposure", conns = conns)$site
subset(columns, column_name %in% c("drug_exposure_start_date",
  "drug_exposure_end_date", "days_supply"),
  select = c(column_name, cdm_datatype, is_date, is_blocked))
column_name cdm_datatype is_date is_blocked
drug_exposure_start_date date TRUE FALSE
drug_exposure_end_date date TRUE FALSE
days_supply integer FALSE FALSE

The two dates delimit the recorded exposure and days_supply describes the supplied duration. These prescribing or dispensing fields do not prove ingestion. They answer a different question from a visit start date.

Exercise 3: test numeric coverage

Does the presence of a measurement table and a value_as_number column guarantee that lab values can be analysed? Check the column itself.

Solution

ds.omop.table.stats("measurement", conns = conns)
#> <dsomop_result>
#> Servers: site
#> Scope: per_site
#>
#> $site
#> $rows
#> [1] 44050
#>
#> $persons
#> [1] 2685

The row band begins at 44,050. The public GiBleed data have exactly 44,053 measurement rows; this analyst call rounds down to its band.

ds.omop.column.stats("measurement", "value_as_number", conns = conns)
#> <dsomop_result>
#> Servers: site
#> Scope: per_site
#>
#> $site
#> $n_total
#> [1] 44050
#>
#> $n_missing
#> [1] 2685
#>
#> $n_distinct
#> [1] 0
#>
#> $n_persons
#> [1] 2685
#>
#> $mean
#> [1] NA
#>
#> $sd
#> [1] NA

n_missing equals n_persons, both 2,685 (the band 2,685–2,689). The same response reports n_distinct = 0: no distinct numeric values are available. The public GiBleed data contain no numeric lab values. Use Synthea27Nj for the lab lessons, and check the chosen lab and unit there before fitting a model.

Recap

A schema tells you which fields exist. Protected counts describe their support. Neither a large row count nor a numeric field guarantees usable lab values.
